title: The Pre-9/11 Put Options: 9.5 Million Transactions, One Bearish Adviser and a Newsletter Faxed on a Sunday
participants: Securities and Exchange Commission, Division of Enforcement
U.S. Attorney’s Office, Eastern District of New York
National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States (staff)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Money was made, and the record says who made it and why. A U.S. investment adviser registered with the SEC, running several hedge funds with $5.3 billion under management, bought 95 percent of the UAL put option volume on 6 September 2001 on a bearish view of the airline industry built on on-time departure figures and AMR’s own disclosed results. A New York hedge fund with $2 billion under management bought more than a third of the UAL puts purchased on 7 September. Subscribers to a California investment-advice newsletter, faxed and emailed on Sunday 9 September, bought AMR puts on the Monday. When the markets reopened on 17 September, AMR fell 40 percent and UAL fell 43 percent, and those positions paid.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What makes an option position look like foreknowledge is the leverage inside it. The Commission’s own staff footnote states the mechanism plainly: people trading illicitly on inside information "often have used options because they allow the trader to leverage an initial investment, so that a relatively small investment can generate huge profits." A high ratio of puts to calls is therefore "a potential indicator of insider trading" — and on 6 September the UAL put volume exceeded call volume by more than twenty times, while on 10 September AMR’s exceeded calls six to one. Those ratios are real. They are also, on the record, the only part of the story that was ever public.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The ratios were published; the account-level data that resolved them was not, and could not be. The fog in this episode runs the other way from the usual: the public could see the volume and never the buyer. Into that gap went the president of the German central bank, Ernst Welteke, whose statements that insider trading had occurred in airline and insurance shares and in gold and oil futures were never confirmed; his own country’s securities regulator said on 27 September 2001 that "there is no evidence that anyone who had knowledge of the attacks before they were committed used it to make financial transactions", and said the same again in December.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There was no windfall to find, and the investigation that looked for one is on the record. From 12 September 2001 the SEC, with the FBI and a Brooklyn prosecutor assigned full time, analysed trading in 103 individual companies and 32 index or exchange-traded funds and examined more than 9.5 million securities transactions, with deliberate redundancy: Large Option Position Reports and Open Interest Distribution Reports that identify holders of large option positions whenever those positions were opened, direct canvasses of twenty of the largest broker-dealers, and the self-regulatory organisations’ own surveillance. The "profits left uncollected" claim was tested against the Options Clearing Corporation, which exercises profitable positions automatically unless a customer instructs otherwise and double-checks any such instruction with the broker: OCC staff recalled no such contact after 9/11.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: This is where the dossier departs from the pattern the atlas usually traces, and it departs from it because the documents do. There is no commission here that narrowed its terms of reference to protect an interest. There is a staff monograph that sets out its method, names the limits of its own authority — "they have not approved this text and it does not necessarily reflect their views" — and reaches a flat negative. What it does not do is name a single adviser, fund, trader or newsletter, or give a single account number; and the SEC memorandum it rests on, "Pre-September 11, 2001 Trading Review" of 15 May 2002, has never been published. A reader who wants to check the conclusion against the underlying data still cannot.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The surveillance architecture built into U.S. securities markets after 1934 and extended through the option-position reporting regime: a market in which, as the monograph puts it, no one can trade "without leaving a paper trail that the SEC can easily access through its regulatory powers".
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The terrorist-financing investigative apparatus stood up after 9/11, and with it the template for every later "trading on terror" claim: a published volume anomaly, an unpublished account-level resolution, and a regulator’s assurance in between.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The claim regenerates itself because the two halves of the evidence sit on opposite sides of a disclosure line. Option volumes and put/call ratios are public and permanent; the identity of the buyer and the rest of their book are not. Anyone can re-derive the anomaly at any time; no one outside the agencies can re-derive the answer.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That someone — al Qaeda, or insiders who were told — loaded up on puts against United and American in the days before 9/11 and made a killing, that some of the winnings were never even collected, and that the proof burned with the SEC’s files in World Trade Center 7.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Every element of it was tested and none survived. The 6 September UAL spike was 95 percent the work of one SEC-registered U.S. adviser running $5.3 billion, whose strategy also had it buying 115,000 AMR shares on 10 September — shares that fell hard when trading resumed; the 7 September UAL buyer was a $2 billion New York fund that held 29,000 UAL shares alongside the puts and came out $85,000 down; the 10 September AMR surge traced to a California newsletter faxed on the Sunday, with 26 of 28 interviewed purchasers citing it; the heavily reported AIG puts were a hedge against 4.2 million shares of AIG held at a low tax basis, on which the fund lost money overall; the offshore $5 million short-side profit belonged to a European speculator who had lost $8 million doing the same thing in the preceding six months. The uncollected-profits story fails on the Options Clearing Corporation’s own mechanics: profitable options exercise automatically unless the customer says otherwise, and the OCC recalled no one saying otherwise. And the WTC 7 argument fails on sequence and custody: the SEC opened this investigation on 12 September 2001 and ran it on exchange, self-regulatory-organisation, broker-dealer and clearing-house records, none of which were kept in that building.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: What the record supports is narrower than the rumour and narrower than a vindication. The volumes were real and anomalous on their face: UAL puts exceeding calls more than twenty to one on 6 September, AMR puts six to one on 10 September. An investigation of genuine scale followed — 103 companies, 32 funds, more than 9.5 million transactions, more than 40 SEC staff, the FBI and a full-time federal prosecutor — and resolved every profitable trade it found to a lawful strategy. The Commission’s own note 130 states the result: "the apparently suspicious consistently proved innocuous." Against that sits what is still not public: no trader, fund or newsletter is named anywhere in the documents, and the SEC memorandum the finding rests on has never been released. The honest ledger entry is that an exhaustive investigation found nothing, and that the public has been asked to take the finding on the word of the people who conducted it.

citations.title: National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States, Monograph on Terrorist Financing (Staff Report to the Commission, 2004) — Appendix B: Securities Trading, pp. 145–151
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Commission's own site and read as extracted text. Appendix B opens: "This appendix describes the staff and U.S. government investigations into the issue of whether anyone with foreknowledge of the 9/11 attacks profited through securities trading, and explains the conclusion in the Commission's final report that extensive government investigation has revealed no evidence of such illicit trading." It records that "Almost since 9/11 itself, there have been consistent reports that massive 'insider trading' preceded the attacks" and that "The Commission has found no evidence to support these reports." On method: the SEC's chief of the Office of Market Surveillance opened an investigation into pre-9/11 trading on 12 September 2001; at a multi-agency meeting at FBI headquarters on 17 September the SEC agreed to lead it; the Department of Justice assigned a white-collar prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Brooklyn full time, who relocated to Washington on 18 September. More than 40 SEC staff were involved at various times, working with the New York Stock Exchange, the American Stock Exchange, NASD Regulation and the Chicago Board Options Exchange; "the investigators analyzed trading in 103 individual companies and 32 index or exchange-traded funds and examined more than 9.5 million securities transactions." The SEC also obtained Large Option Position Reports and Open Interest Distribution Reports, "that identified the holders of substantial amounts of options without regard to when those options were purchased", contacted 20 of the largest broker-dealers directly and asked the Securities Industry Association to canvass its members. On the three trades most cited in the press: on 6 September the UAL put volume "exceeded the call option volume by more than 20 times", and "The SEC quickly discovered, however, that a single U.S. investment adviser had purchased 95 percent of the UAL put option volume for the day", an adviser "based in the United States, registered with the SEC, and managed several hedge funds with $5.3 billion under management", whose stated reasons included "recently released on-time departure figures" and "recently disclosed news by AMR reflecting poor business fundamentals", and which "also bought 115,000 shares of AMR on September 10" that "dropped significantly when the markets reopened"; the SEC referred the trade to the FBI anyway and the FBI "reached the same conclusion". On 10 September the AMR put volume "exceeded the call volume by a ratio of 6:1", and the SEC "traced much of the surge in volume to a California investment advice newsletter, distributed by email and fax on Sunday, September 9", interviewing 28 purchasers of whom 26 cited the newsletter, with another 27 purchasers listed as its subscribers. On 7 September a single trader bought "more than one-third of the total puts purchased that day" in UAL and was identified as "a well-established New York hedge fund with $2 billion under management" that also held 29,000 UAL shares and "actually lost $85,000 in value when the market reopened". A heavily reported AIG put purchase was found by the FBI to be a hedge of "a long position of 4.2 million shares in the AIG common stock" held at a very low tax basis, on which the fund "overall lost money as a result of the attacks". On the claim that profits went uncollected, the monograph records that officials at the SEC and the Options Clearing Corporation stated that "any profitable options positions are automatically exercised upon the expiration date unless the customer explicitly directed otherwise", that the OCC double-checks any such instruction with the broker, and that "The OCC personnel had no recollection of any such contacts after 9/11." It records that when the markets opened on 17 September "AMR fell 40 percent and UAL fell 43 percent." On the international side it records that a European regulator traced a $5 million offshore short-side profit to "an extremely wealthy European national who often speculated by taking short positions in the U.S. market" and who "had employed this strategy to lose $8 million in the six months preceding 9/11", and that on 27 September 2001 a spokesman for the German regulator BAWe declared that "there is no evidence that anyone who had knowledge of the attacks before they were committed used it to make financial transactions." WHAT THE DOCUMENT IS AND IS NOT: its own preface states "This is a study by Commission staff. While the Commissioners have been briefed on the work and have had the opportunity to review earlier drafts of some of this work, they have not approved this text and it does not necessarily reflect their views." It names no trader, adviser, hedge fund or newsletter, gives no account numbers, and says nothing whatever about World Trade Center 7 or about any record destroyed there.

citations.title: The 9/11 Commission Report (Final Report of the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States) — note 130 to chapter 5, p. 499
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. Note 130 to chapter 5, printed at page 499, is the Commission's own statement on the question: "Highly publicized allegations of insider trading in advance of 9/11 generally rest on reports of unusual pre-9/11 trading activity in companies whose stock plummeted after the attacks. Some unusual trading did in fact occur, but each such trade proved to have an innocuous explanation. For example, the volume of put options — investments that pay off only when a stock drops in price — surged in the parent companies of United Airlines on September 6 and American Airlines on September 10 — highly suspicious trading on its face. Yet, further investigation has revealed that the trading had no connection with 9/11. A single U.S.-based institutional investor with no conceivable ties to al Qaeda purchased 95 percent of the UAL puts on September 6 as part of a trading strategy that also included buying 115,000 shares of American on September 10. Similarly, much of the seemingly suspicious trading in American on September 10 was traced to a specific U.S.-based options trading newsletter, faxed to its subscribers on Sunday, September 9, which recommended these trades. These examples typify the evidence examined by the investigation. The SEC and the FBI, aided by other agencies and the securities industry, devoted enormous resources to investigating this issue, including securing the cooperation of many foreign governments. These investigators have found that the apparently suspicious consistently proved innocuous." The note's own sourcing line cites interviews with Joseph Cella, an FBI briefing, and an SEC memorandum from the Division of Enforcement to the Chair and Commissioners titled "Pre-September 11, 2001 Trading Review", dated May 15, 2002. That memorandum is not public and was not read here; what is read here is the Commission's characterisation of it.
